headline: Exogenous HGH
punch: The part your bloodwork cannot see.

headline: The model everyone uses
body: So the standard picture is a straight line. You inject GH, it travels to your liver, your liver makes *IGF-1*, that IGF-1 goes out into your blood, reaches the growth plate, and you grow. Which is exactly why every protocol you have ever read tracks serum IGF-1 as the scoreboard. If that line were the whole story then your blood IGF-1 would be a direct readout of how much growing you are doing. | There is a 1982 experiment that breaks the line, and the design is so simple you will wonder why nobody shows it to you.
punch: Inject, measure IGF-1, assume growth. That is the model.

headline: Isaksson 1982
body: They took rats and removed the pituitary, so the animals made zero GH of their own. Then they injected GH **directly into the growth plate of one tibia only**. The other leg got nothing. | Now think about what that controls for. Same animal, same heart, same bloodstream, same circulating IGF-1 washing past both legs at the identical concentration every second. The only difference between that rat's two legs was which one had hormone put into it locally. **The injected leg grew more.**
punch: ==One bloodstream. Two legs. Two different outcomes.==

headline: What the authors concluded
body: Their exact wording: this finding suggests growth hormone **directly stimulates the cells in the growth plate**, and **does not support the theory** that the increase in plasma somatomedin following GH administration is the cause of this stimulation. | Somatomedin is just the old name for IGF-1, so translate that sentence into modern language and they are saying the blood number is not the mechanism. In 1982. That is the year this was already known, and it has been quietly ignored by every protocol since.
punch: _The leg that got the hormone grew. Blood levels were identical._

headline: Loveridge ran it backwards
subhead: BLOCKING GH INSTEAD OF ADDING IT
body: Thirteen years later Loveridge did the opposite experiment. Instead of adding GH they took it away, using an antiserum raised against the rat's own growth hormone, and then watched what happened inside the growth plate. | The plate narrowed. The proliferative zone shrank and the total number of chondrocytes synthesising DNA dropped. So the growth genuinely broke. And the whole time, **circulating IGF-1 was unchanged**: 10.3 against 10.7 nmol/l at 4 days, which is noise. | What this means is that you can break growth without the blood marker registering anything at all.
punch: ==They broke the growth. The blood number never moved.==

headline: So what is the real variable?
body: *Local IGF-1* is the answer, and the distinction matters more than anything else in this post. The growth plate manufactures its own IGF-1, right there in the tissue, under GH control. That pool is made and used in the same place and it never enters general circulation in a way a blood test can see. | So there are two separate IGF-1 pools. The one your liver makes, which you measure. And the one the plate makes for itself, which you cannot. Lui 2010 is the experiment that proves which of the two does the work.
punch: Two pools. You only ever measure one of them.

headline: Lui 2010
subhead: THE CLEANEST EXPERIMENT IN THE FIELD
body: They engineered two versions of the same IGF-1 protein. One was fused to an antibody fragment that binds matrilin-3, a cartilage protein, so it sticks to the growth plate and concentrates there. The other was identical IGF-1 with no targeting at all. Same molecule, same dose, same animal model. | The cartilage-targeted version grew bone. The **non-targeted IGF-1 did not show any significant effect on growth** whatsoever. | What this means is that the variable was never how much IGF-1 is present. It was where the IGF-1 ends up.
punch: _It is not how much. It is where._

headline: GH and IGF-1 split the job
body: Here is how the labour divides inside the plate. The *germinal layer*, meaning the reserve cells sitting at the very top, carries the highest concentration of GH receptors of any zone. GH's job there is to commit those reserve cells into the dividing pool. | Then locally produced IGF-1 takes over and drives the actual dividing in the proliferative zone below. So GH recruits and local IGF-1 multiplies, which is why blocking GH shrank the proliferative zone in Loveridge's experiment even though the labelling index per cell did not change. Fewer cells were being recruited into it.

headline: Hunziker measured every stage
body: This study is the most complete accounting of what each hormone does at the cell level. Rats with no pituitary, then either IGF-1 or GH, then measure how long one cell cycle takes at each stage of the plate. | Reserve cell cycle time with no pituitary: **50 days**. With IGF-1: **15 days**. With GH: **8 days**. For comparison a normal rat sits at 6. | Dividing cells: 11 days untreated, down to 4.5 with IGF-1 and **3** with GH. Hypertrophic phase: 6 days down to 4 and **2.8**. GH beat IGF-1 at every single stage measured.

headline: And here is the inversion
body: GH achieved all of that **while producing a lower level of circulating IGF-1** than the group that was given IGF-1 directly. Read that again. Lower blood number, more growth, same experiment, same animals. | That is now the second time in this post that serum IGF-1 moved in the opposite direction to actual bone growth. Loveridge was the first. This is the second. And if a marker can move opposite to the thing it is supposed to measure, then it is not measuring that thing.
punch: _Twice now. The marker goes down, the growth goes up._

headline: The actual engine is cell size
body: Most people assume growth is about cells dividing more. It is mostly not. Hypertrophy, the final swelling of a chondrocyte just before it dies and is replaced by bone, is described in that paper as **the most efficient cellular process contributing to bone elongation**. | The numbers: terminal cell height went from **19.5 µm** untreated to **26.5 µm** on GH, with a normal rat at 29.8. Mean cell volume went from **6,370** to **11,140 µm³**, where a normal rat sits at 10,246. And GH raised cell productivity **5 to 7 fold** at the stem and dividing stages.
punch: The plate grows by cells getting bigger, not just dividing more.

headline: Does it burn your plates?
body: This is the question everyone actually wants answered, so here is the best data on it. Nwosu 2021 followed **71 children** on growth hormone for between 2 and 14 years, mean 5.5, and tracked skeletal maturation the whole way. | Bone age minus chronological age at the start was **-1.05**. At the end of therapy it was **-0.69**. **P = 0.09**, which is not a significant change. | Notice they were negative at both ends. These children were behind schedule and they stayed behind schedule.
punch: ==Long-term GH did not advance skeletal maturation.==

headline: Be precise about that
body: There was a real catch-up effect, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Piecewise regression found bone age gaining about **1.5 months per year** of therapy for the first 6.5 years. Then it plateaued and the net change across the whole course was not significant. | Mauras found the same shape in a randomised trial: bone ages advanced about **1 year per chronological year in both** the standard dose and the double dose group, and the paper states high dose GH **did not increase the rate of skeletal maturation**.
punch: A small early catch-up, then nothing.

headline: 83,803 children
body: KIGS collected every child treated with that manufacturer's growth hormone between 1987 and 2012. This is not a trial, it is the entire real-world record, and the median gain in near-adult height is reported in SDS. | GH deficiency: **1.79** in boys, **2.07** in girls. Idiopathic short stature: **1.37** and **1.62**. Small for gestational age: **1.34** and **1.57**. Turner syndrome: **1.07** in girls. | Notice the pattern. The group whose axis was genuinely broken gains roughly double what the merely short group gains from the same drug.
punch: _Fixing a deficiency beats topping up a working axis._

headline: Why the dose stops paying
body: Mauras randomised GH-deficient adolescents to **0.3 versus 0.7 mg/kg per week** and followed them to near-adult height. More than double the dose bought **4.6 cm**, P < 0.001, n = 75. Ranke's 2021 review summarises the same trial the same way, at about 4 cm for a doubling. | And it was not free. At any given time roughly **28%** of the high dose group had IGF-1 above the normal range against **9%** on standard dose, with greater rises in fasting insulin, P = 0.011. The curve bends, and the cost shows up in insulin rather than in bone age.

headline: Putting it together
body: GH acts on the growth plate directly, not only through your liver, and that has been known since 1982. The IGF-1 pool that drives growth is made locally inside the plate and is invisible on bloodwork. Serum IGF-1 has now moved opposite to real growth in two separate experiments in this post alone. | Bone age did not meaningfully run ahead at therapeutic doses, across 71 children followed up to 14 years. And the largest gains land in people whose axis was actually broken, not in people topping up a working one.
punch: ==Stop reading serum IGF-1 as your growth number.==
